text:
Every chart today is drawn from one retail series










Monthly retail sales in Victoria, Australia, in millions of dollars
441 months, April 1982 to December 2018, no gaps and no missing values


Say what the data is before any model touches it, because every chart for the next two lectures is drawn from this one series and the room should be able to name it. Victorian takeaway food turnover: how much Australians spent on takeaway in one state, month by month, measured in millions of dollars. The y axis on every chart today is those millions.
Point at the shape while it is bare. It grows about sixfold, the swings grow with it, and December is the spike. All three facts come back later: the growth is what defeats the seasonal naive, the growing swings are what defeat the Gaussian interval, and December is what defeats the plain naive.
Leave the split for the next slide. This one is the series, bare.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: The last 24 months are held out, and never shuffled
text:
The last 24 months are held out, and never shuffled










Split in time, never at random: a shuffle trains on 2018 to predict 2017
\(h = 24\) came from the decision, not from the data: a two-year plan needs two years


train, test = D.train_test(spine, h=24)


Every number in the next two lectures rests on this slide, so say both the rule and the reason out loud.
The rule: the split is chronological. The train_test_split everybody has typed a hundred times shuffles rows, which here hands the model 2018 and asks it about 2017 - a score that comes back excellent and meaningless. Lecture 2 returns to this as leakage, with two subtler versions.
Then h. Twenty-four is a planning choice, not a statistical one: this series is used for two-year budgeting. If the decision were quarterly, h would be 3 and a different model might win. Ask the room what horizon their work needs.
Say the last line as a discipline: the test set is spent once. Everything to lecture 2 is fitted on the 417 months, and the 24 are looked at only when there is a score to report.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Every formula here is built from four symbols
text:
Every formula here is built from four symbols







Symbol
Meaning




\(T\)
the forecast origin, the last observed time


\(h\)
the forecast horizon, steps ahead


\(m\)
the seasonal period, 12 for monthly data


\(\hat{y}_{a\mid b}\)
the forecast of time \(a\), made from data up to time \(b\)




The origin stays at \(T\) all segment, so we drop the bar and write \(\hat{y}_{T+h}\). It comes back whenever the origin moves.


Four symbols carry the whole segment, and the room already knows two of them from Day 1. T is where we stand, h is how far ahead we look, m is the length of one cycle. Every formula in this segment uses nothing else.
Spend a sentence on the bar, because it is the only one that is new and it is the one that trips people later. Read it out loud as “of, given”: y-hat T+h given T is the forecast of the value at T+h, made knowing everything up to T. Segment A never moves the origin, so the bar is dropped there and the formulas stay short. The residual slide needs y-hat t given t-1, one step from yesterday, and segment E needs e t+h given t, where the origin slides. Same notation, three uses.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Three baselines start by ignoring the calendar
text:
Three baselines start by ignoring the calendar
The mean. Average everything, use it for every horizon:
\[\hat{y}_{T+h} = \bar{y} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} y_t\]

The naive. Take the last observation, use it for every horizon:
\[\hat{y}_{T+h} = y_T\]


The drift. The naive, tilted by the line through the first and last point:
\[\hat{y}_{T+h} = y_T + \dfrac{h}{T-1}(y_T - y_1)\]

45 seconds each, and they are a set, not items 1-3 of a list of four: none of them has a term for the calendar, and that shared blind spot is what the next four slides are about.
The mean uses all T observations, so on a series that has grown sixfold it sits far below where the series is now. The naive uses one observation, which at least puts it at the right level. The drift is the naive with a slope bolted on - the line through the first and last observation, extended.
Point at drift’s denominator, because it returns in segment C: T-1 rather than T because T observations have T-1 gaps between them, and that same T-1 turns up in its interval width formula for exactly the same reason.
Read the card and stop. The room should be able to tell you, before the next slide, that none of them can produce a December.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Two of the three at least start in the right place
text:
Two of the three at least start in the right place










Point at the flat pink line first. That is the mean, and on a series that has grown sixfold it is visibly hopeless, which is the point of showing it. It is not a straw man: it is the reason a scale-free metric exists at all, and lecture 2 uses it.
The green naive line is flat too, but it starts from the right place. Then the drift, which is the only line on the slide with any growth in it - and ask the room what month the drift line thinks it is. It has no idea, and you can see that it has no idea, because it is straight.
Ask which one they would rather ship, then ask what is still wrong with the best of the three. The answer they will give, in some form, is that these are straight lines through data that is obviously not straight. Hold that thought: the next three slides turn it into a measurement.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Residuals flatter, forecast errors do not
text:
Residuals flatter, forecast errors do not
Residual (\(e_t\)): one-step error on training data
\[e_t = y_t - \hat{y}_{t|t-1}\]



Residuals (\(e_t\))

In-sample training errors
Flattering to the model




Forecast Errors (\(e_{T+h}\))

Out-of-sample holdout errors
Honest evidence





Naive: \(e_t = y_t - y_{t-1}\), the raw one-step change.


The holdout has not happened yet. The only evidence a model has already given you is what it got wrong on the training data, and that is what we are about to read.
The bar is the one from the notation table, with the origin moved: yhat_{t|t-1} is the forecast of y_t made from data up to t-1.
Residuals flatter, forecast errors do not. Everything in this segment is residuals. Everything in lecture 2 is forecast errors.
For the naive the residual is simple subtraction: this step minus the one before. That is what makes it possible to say where the error came from, rather than only how big it was.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: The naive’s errors still know what month it is
text:
The naive’s errors still know what month it is










Lags 12 and 24 (orange) stand at 0.68 and 0.58, against a bound of 0.10
Day 1 named that shape: a spike every \(m\) lags is seasonality, still in there


The first diagnosis of the day and the template for every one after, so go slowly. Send them back to Day 1’s table of five ACF shapes first - it was built to read a series and reads residuals unchanged, because residuals are just another series.
Ask what shape is on the screen and wait. Somebody will say the spikes at 12 and 24, and that is the entire finding: the seasonal pattern went through the model and came out untouched.
Say the size out loud, because “significant” is doing real work. Bounds at plus or minus 0.10; the orange spikes at 0.68 and 0.58, six or seven times that. Not a marginal call.
Land the card, noting the fix was named by the diagnostic rather than guessed at. Somebody usually asks whether drift’s slope handles this - take a show of hands before you turn the slide.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Drift fixes the mean and nothing else
text:
Drift fixes the mean and nothing else










Drift’s residual is the naive’s, less the constant slope 0.77: same spread, same every lag
Mean residual moves from +0.77 to +0.00, and lags 12 and 24 do not move at all
A trend term fixed the bias. It could not fix a fault that was never about trend


Two correlograms that are the same picture - let the room hunt for the difference before you say there is not one. The only thing that moves is the number under each panel: +0.77 to +0.00. Every bar is identical.
The algebra is one line, worth the board. Drift’s fitted value is last month plus a fixed slope, so its residual is the naive’s shifted down by a constant - exactly, to machine precision. A constant shift changes the mean and nothing else, which is why the spreads match to four figures and every autocorrelation is identical.
So drift did what it was asked and zeroed the bias, and the spikes at 12 and 24 sit where they sat, because a straight line has nothing to say about December.
That closes the question the last slide opened: the tilt we had does not buy a calendar. Note what just got spent - drift is the only benchmark with a trend term and it is now behind us, which is the reason segment B exists.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: The seasonal naive repeats last year’s same month
text:
The seasonal naive repeats last year’s same month
\[\hat{y}_{T+h} = y_{T+h-m(k+1)}, \qquad k = \left\lfloor \frac{h-1}{m} \right\rfloor\]
Monthly data, so \(m = 12\): one seasonal cycle is one year.

\(k+1\) is how many seasonal cycles back the forecast reaches
\(h = 1 \dots 12\): \(k = 0\), so it copies last year’s same month
\(h = 13 \dots 24\): \(k = 1\), so it steps back a second year



The staircase in segment C is built on this \(k\): flat within each block of \(m = 12\) months, one step up per seasonal cycle.


Say m out loud before the formula: the data is monthly, so one cycle is 12 months, and m = 12 everywhere in this deck. Everything else on the slide is that substitution.
k is zero whenever the horizon stays inside one cycle, so for h up to 12 the seasonal naive is just “last year’s same month”. k only starts counting at h = 13, and that is exactly where its prediction interval takes its first step up. At h = 24 it is still 1, so the second year is copied whole: k changes once per cycle, not once per step. Segment C uses the same k for the same reason, so give this slide a real minute: the staircase later has no floor without it.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: All four simple models, and the floor they set
text:
All four simple models, and the floor they set










Objective evidence: what proves a complex model adds value.


The full picture, and the one to photograph. One line added to the earlier chart, and it is the first forecast today with the shape of the data in it - let the room see the orange track the December peaks before any number is quoted.
Name what just happened, because it is the method of the whole segment: we did not pick this model, the residual ACF picked it. Read the error, name the missing term, add it, look again.
The room now has four models and two visible facts: one has the season, another has the trend, none has both. Do not resolve it - the residual check two slides on earns the resolution.
Turn the card into a question to take back to work: what is the simple baseline, and by how much did we beat it? Ask a senior room whether their last model review answered it.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Fit four models at once in code
text:
Fit four models at once in code
from statsforecast import StatsForecast
from statsforecast.models import (HistoricAverage, Naive,
                                  SeasonalNaive, RandomWalkWithDrift)

sf = StatsForecast(models=[HistoricAverage(), Naive(),
                           SeasonalNaive(season_length=12),
                           RandomWalkWithDrift()], freq=D.FREQ)
fc = sf.forecast(df=train, h=H, level=[80, 95], fitted=True)
fv = sf.forecast_fitted_values()      # the residuals we just read

Four models, about four lines each, no tuning, one second to run. This is the cell exercise 2.1 opens with.
The one argument to point at is fitted=True, because it is the difference between a forecast and a diagnosis. Without it you get fc and nothing else; with it, forecast_fitted_values gives you the in-sample fitted values whose residuals the last five slides were built on.
On many series the seasonal naive is genuinely tough to beat, and by the end of today they will have watched it beat a decomposition model over eight folds. Do not let these sound like toys.
Then flag the turn: the floor is set, and the rest of the segment asks one question - is the winner any good?

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: The winner’s residuals sit high and fan out
text:
The winner’s residuals sit high and fan out



































The dashed line is the mean, +7.9: 68% of the errors sit above zero




Each box is a decade’s typical miss: 8.5, then 26.2, 3x as tall



Put the bare panel up and say nothing. Ask what is wrong with it before you click - both faults are visible with no annotation, which is why the slide arrives with nothing drawn on it.
The first answer will be that it sits mostly above zero. Click once: the mean line and its bullet arrive together, so their answer is now drawn on the picture they gave it about. The second fault needs a prompt - the left third is thin, the right third is tall. Click again for the boxes.
Say what the boxes are, because “SD” alone is a statistic and this is a quantity: each is a typical month’s miss drawn as a height, in the millions the y axis is in. Early on the model was out by about 8.5; by the 2010s, 26.2. The right box is 3x the height of the left, and that height is the finding.
Do not name the four properties or diagnose either fault here - segment B’s grid does that once, at the end. But say the two are going to different places. The next slide takes the bias. The widening is not a missing-term problem, nothing in segment A will touch it, and it is why one sigma cannot size a band. Tell the room you are parking it, so nobody waits for a fix.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: The season is gone, but the decay is not
text:
The season is gone, but the decay is not










Lags 12 and 24 (orange) now fall inside the bounds at -0.03 and +0.04
The orange spikes the naive had are gone: the calendar term worked
What is left decays smoothly from 0.85. Day 1 named that shape too: trend


Say the comparison out loud - the pair is the argument. Earlier the orange lags were 0.68 and 0.58; now -0.03 and +0.04, both inside the bounds. Students skate past that, so make it count: it is the first time today a diagnosis has been confirmed by a later measurement rather than asserted.
Then the black bars: a smooth decay from 0.85. Same table, different row. The season came out completely and something with the trend signature stayed in.
That also answers the panel’s first fault. A model with no growth term under-forecasts a growing series, so the errors sit above zero and the mean is +7.9. The correlogram named the missing term; the mean residual measured what it costs.
Now the reason drift was spent early. A missing term is named and no benchmark on the list supplies it: drift has the slope and cannot produce a December, the seasonal naive has the calendar and cannot grow, and neither patches into the other. The next model is a different kind of object, and that is segment B. Take the card from the room rather than reading it to them.
If asked why r_1 is near 1: neighbouring months share almost all of their shortfall, because the level moves slowly. It decays to nothing by lag 11 because eleven months is long enough for the level to have moved on.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Decomposition is also a forecasting method
text:
Decomposition is also a forecasting method
1 · STL splits the series, and the three parts group into two:
\[y_t = \underbrace{T_t + R_t}_{A_t,\;\text{seasonally adjusted}} + \underbrace{S_t}_{\text{season}}\]

2 · Forecast each part with the simple model that suits it:
\[\underbrace{\hat{A}_{T+h} = A_T + \frac{h}{T-1}(A_T - A_1)}_{\text{drift}}
\qquad
\underbrace{\hat{S}_{T+h} = S_{T+h-m(k+1)}}_{\text{seasonal naive}}\]


3 · Add them back:
\[\hat{y}_{T+h} = \hat{A}_{T+h} + \hat{S}_{T+h}\]



MSTL(season_length=12, trend_forecaster=RandomWalkWithDrift()) runs all three steps in one call.


The answer the room worked out just before the divider. Build it one fragment at a time, saying the step before showing the algebra.
Step 1 is Day 1’s decomposition regrouped: trend plus remainder is the seasonally adjusted series A_t, and S_t is everything else. If anyone reads T_t as the forecast origin, that is Day 1’s trend-cycle - subscripted t, one value per time step, not the single origin T.
Step 2 is the payoff, so point at it rather than reading it. Both formulas are benchmarks they already have with y swapped for a part, and they are the exact two the residual checks named: drift on the part with trend and no season, the seasonal naive on the part that is nothing but season. Each model is finally pointed at the component it is good at.
Step 3 adds them back, and the card says it is one constructor call.
trend_forecaster is pinned to drift on purpose - the default is AutoETS (Day 3), and no Day 3 model should quietly win a Day 2 comparison.
The plus sign assumes additive seasonality; multiplicative is handled by logging first.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: STL’s two parts forecast separately, then add
text:
STL’s two parts forecast separately, then add










Walk the three panels from top to bottom: 1. Top panel: Seasonally adjusted series A_t. Drift extends it with a growth line. 2. Middle panel: Seasonal component S_t. Seasonal naive repeats last year’s shape. 3. Bottom panel: Summing both yields the recombined MSTL forecast (sky blue).
The two top panels are the two diagnoses of segment A, drawn as pictures.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: On this window, the decomposition route clears the floor
text:
On this window, the decomposition route clears the floor










The seasonal naive repeats last year’s level; STL lets drift carry the growth.


Let the graph do the talking: the room should see the STL route tracking the actuals closer before any number is quoted. No score on this slide, lecture 2 defines the metric and scores it.
Do not let this land as “STL wins”. It wins on THIS window. Lecture 2 scores it over eight rolling origins and the ordering flips. Flag that now, so the reversal reads as the lesson rather than as a contradiction.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Ljung-Box turns 24 lag checks into one test
text:
Ljung-Box turns 24 lag checks into one test
\(H_0\): the first \(\ell = 24\) residual autocorrelations are all zero.
\[Q = T(T+2)\sum_{k=1}^{\ell}\frac{r_k^2}{T-k}
\qquad Q \sim \chi^2_{\ell-K} \; \text{ under } H_0\]
\(r_k\): the lag-\(k\) autocorrelation · \(K\): parameters estimated, 0 here · \(p\): how often a \(Q\) this large would happen if \(H_0\) were true

\(p < 0.05\): autocorrelation is real \(\rightarrow\) model is not finished
\(p \ge 0.05\): residuals are indistinguishable from white noise


Motivation from Day 1: with 24 individual lag bounds at 95%, expecting 1 spike by chance is normal. Every ACF this segment read was read by eye, and by eye is fine when a spike is seven times the bound. Ljung-Box pools all lags into a single test so the call does not have to be made by eye: - H_0: all autocorrelations up to lag l are zero. - Rule of thumb: l = 24 for seasonal monthly data (2m), K = 0 for benchmarks (no estimated params). - p is a probability, not a size: it says how surprising this Q would be if the residuals really were white noise.
One sentence of warning before the next slide, because it prevents the misreading that slide invites: this is a pass/fail on whether a model is finished. It is not a score, and it does not rank models.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Every baseline fails, and they fail differently
text:
Every baseline fails, and they fail differently










Every \(p\) is far below 0.05: not one of the five is finished
Read the shapes, not the \(p\): annual spikes mean a missing season, decay means a missing trend
STL + drift halves the spread, 12.7 to 6.5, and still fails: see lag 24
The residual checklist is four: uncorrelated · zero mean · constant variance · normal


Five panels in teaching order, left to right, so the eye walks the lecture’s path. Mean fails everything. Naive leaves the orange spikes. Seasonal naive kills the spikes and leaves the decay. Drift is the naive again. STL plus drift is the only panel with neither.
Head off the misreading: a room reading a p column will rank by it. The seasonal naive has the smallest p of the four benchmarks and is the best of them - its one-step residual is a year-on-year change, the naive’s is month-on-month, so the two are not comparable. The column is pass/fail; the ranking comes from lecture 2.
Do not oversell the last panel. STL plus drift is the best-behaved residual of the day and still not white noise: p is about 7e-06, and if asked where that comes from, point at the one orange bar at lag 24 below the bound. That gap is Day 3’s opening.
Read the four verdicts off the last bullet, do not re-teach them. Uncorrelated and zero mean failed, constant variance failed, normal is untested and segment C opens with it. Say the split as an instruction: the first two are messages about the model, so go back and change it. Constant variance leaves the point forecast alone, so there is nothing to change - a different kind of finding, not a lesser one, and the reason one sigma cannot size a band.
A stats-literate room reaches for a transform before you offer it. Logs, or Box-Cox at the spine’s lambda of about 0.07, would take constant variance off the list. Real fix, deliberately not today’s: today is what to do when the width is wrong. Day 3 opens with the transform.
Exercise 2.2 runs this checklist on the drift method.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: The future is a range, not a point
text:
The future is a range, not a point
At origin \(T\) the future value is still random; capital \(Y\) marks a value not yet observed:
\[Y_{T+h}\mid \mathcal{I}_T
\qquad \mathcal{I}_T = \text{everything known at time } T\]

Point forecast: one centre, usually a mean or median
80% interval: the \(0.1\) and \(0.9\) quantiles of \(Y_{T+h}\mid \mathcal{I}_T\)
95% interval: the \(0.025\) and \(0.975\) quantiles



The distribution belongs to the unknown future value, not to the forecast. What a quantile is


Decisions like staffing buffers, warehouse capacity, and safety inventory depend directly on the interval width. We produce one point forecast, but we do not believe the future must equal that point. Before it is observed, we represent the future as plausible outcomes conditional on what we know now. The point forecast is one summary; an interval takes two quantiles. The rest of the deck asks how to construct them.
The three methods differ in how they get the quantiles: impose a Gaussian shape, simulate futures from empirical errors, or calibrate a set from past forecast errors. The point forecast stays the same throughout; only the band changes.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: The seasonal naive’s prediction interval
text:
The seasonal naive’s prediction interval










Make the room read the dashed actual line against the bands rather than admiring the shading. Ask how many of the 24 points fall inside the 80% band. It looks excellent here, and lecture 2 shows a single 24-point window cannot measure a coverage rate at all.
One sentence if you want one: the interval is the forecast, and the line down the middle is just its most likely value.
Plant one thing without explaining it - the band is flat through 2017 then steps out at the start of 2018. Point, say “we will come back to that”, move on. Two slides later the recursion says why, and the room recognizes it rather than being told.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Every model says: something known, plus an error
text:
Every model says: something known, plus an error
Segment A defined a residual as a subtraction:
\[e_t = y_t - \hat{y}_{t|t-1}\]

Move the forecast across, and the same line becomes a recipe for making data:
\[y_t = \hat{y}_{t|t-1} + e_t\]



Every interval method in this deck is one answer to the same question: where does \(e_t\) come from?


One line of algebra the room can do in its head, so do it in front of them. Write the residual definition, move the forecast across, stop.
Read the second line as a recipe: any value is the forecast we could have made plus the error we then made. True by construction for every model here, which is why what follows applies to all five, not just the seasonal naive.
The card is the map for the next twenty minutes - put it up and leave it up. The three methods only disagree about where e comes from: a normal with SD sigma-hat (segment C), the errors this model already made (D), or nothing specified and calibrate instead (E).
Name the promotion out loud - it is the real move and easy to skate past. Until this slide a model was a rule for producing a number; now it is a claim about how the series is made. Every derivation from here is arithmetic on that sentence.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: The Gaussian interval is a spread times a multiplier
text:
The Gaussian interval is a spread times a multiplier
The Gaussian answer to that question, in one line:
\[e_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) \;\text{ i.i.d.}\]

Grant it, and the interval closes into a formula:
\[\hat{y}_{T+1|T} \pm c\,\hat{\sigma}
\qquad\text{with}\qquad
\hat{\sigma} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T - K - M}\sum_{t=1}^{T} e_t^2}\]

\(c\) comes off that normal: 1.28 for an 80% band, 1.96 for 95%
\(K\) and \(M\) shrink the denominator: parameters estimated, and residuals a model cannot form

What a standard deviation is

Read the first line as the answer to the question left up on the last slide: the error comes from a normal, centred on zero, one spread for every t. Grant that and the formula is arithmetic. Flag that the line is doing more work than it looks - three claims are packed into it and the slide two on takes them out one at a time. Plant it and move.
Two ingredients. The spread is the SD of the one-step residuals; the multiplier comes off the normal above it. The assumption supplies the shape, the residuals supply the size.
K and M are named and not spelled out on purpose - neither appears anywhere else in the course. One sentence each if asked. K is 0 for all four benchmarks, none of which estimates a parameter. M is the residuals a model cannot form: a seasonal naive has no year before its first to copy, so its first 12 months get no fitted value, leaving 405 residuals from 417 training months. Undercounting them - dividing by T instead - makes sigma-hat too small and the band too narrow, which is hard to spot because the numbers still look plausible.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: The formula was one step. What about \(h\)?
text:
The formula was one step. What about \(h\)?
\(\hat{\sigma}\) measures one-step errors. Put the naive’s forecast into the recipe:
\[y_t = y_{t-1} + e_t, \qquad e_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) \;\text{ i.i.d.}\]

Roll it forward. Each step carries one more error:
\[\begin{aligned}
y_{T+1} &= y_T + e_{T+1} \\
y_{T+2} &= y_T + e_{T+1} + e_{T+2} \\
y_{T+h} &= y_T + \textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{h} e_{T+i}
\end{aligned}\]


The forecast is \(y_T\), so the error is that whole sum, and independent errors add variances:
\[\operatorname{Var}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{h} e_{T+i}\Big) = h\,\sigma^2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \hat{\sigma}_h = \hat{\sigma}\sqrt{h}\]

Board pace, not slide pace. The only derivation in the deck, and it pays for the whole next slide - let the room watch each line appear.
Ask the title before you answer it. Sigma-hat was built from one-step residuals, so the last slide’s band is a one-step band, and the chart they have already seen runs out to twenty-four.
The first line is the recipe with one substitution: the naive’s forecast for t is y_{t-1}, so y_t = y_{t-1} + e_t. Nothing new is assumed about the model, only about e. Same e as segment A, worth ten seconds: e_t was measured on training data, e_{T+1} is the same object at a time we have not reached. No new symbol.
Roll it forward and let them count. One step, one error; two steps, two. The pattern is visible before the third line lands, so ask for it.
Land the last line deliberately: the VARIANCE is h sigma squared, not the standard deviation. Independent things add variances. Square root at the end and sigma root h falls out - which is why every formula on the next slide has a square root in it.
If asked whether the errors really are independent: they are not, segment B measured exactly that, and the slide after next names all three assumptions. Bank the question and let it arrive.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Each model accumulates errors at its own rate
text:
Each model accumulates errors at its own rate
Run that same count on each model’s own recursion:







Model
\(h\)-step forecast standard deviation




Naive
\(\hat{\sigma}_h = \hat{\sigma}\sqrt{h}\)


Mean
\(\hat{\sigma}_h = \hat{\sigma}\sqrt{1 + 1/T}\)


Seasonal naive
\(\hat{\sigma}_h = \hat{\sigma}\sqrt{k+1}\),   \(k = \lfloor (h-1)/m \rfloor\)


Drift
\(\hat{\sigma}_h = \hat{\sigma}\sqrt{h\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{T-1}\right)}\)




Seasonal naive: \(y_t = y_{t-m} + e_t\), so reaching \(T+h\) crosses \(k+1\) seasonal cycles, not \(h\) steps
Mean and drift carry an extra term because their centre is estimated, not copied


Say this first and the table stops being four things to memorise: every row is the previous slide’s argument run on a different recursion.
The seasonal naive is the same count over a different lag - stepping back by m from T+h lands on observed data after k+1 hops, not h, so k+1 errors accumulate. That is the staircase, and why the band is flat inside a year. Send them back to the fan chart: the step they were told to notice is this k going from 0 to 1.
The mean’s 1 + 1/T is one variance for the noise plus one T-th for not knowing the true mean. Drift’s T-1 is the gaps its slope was averaged over - more history, less added by extrapolating. Both estimate their centre, which the naive and seasonal naive never do, and that is what the extra term buys.
Do not read the formulas out; they are in the cheatsheet. The claim is the title.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: The Gaussian interval rests on three assumptions
text:
The Gaussian interval rests on three assumptions
One line did all of it: \(e_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\) i.i.d.

Residuals are uncorrelated: otherwise \(\hat{\sigma}\) understates the spread
Residuals have constant variance: one \(\hat{\sigma}\) for the whole series
Residuals are normally distributed: otherwise \(c = 1.28\) is the wrong multiplier



Segment A failed the first two by looking. The third has never been checked.


Read the three out of the line the sigma-hat slide put up: i.i.d. is independent, so uncorrelated; identically distributed with one sigma is constant variance; the N is normal. The room wrote that line down two slides ago without noticing it was a list of assumptions - which is exactly how it happens in practice.
Count them off on your fingers; the next two segments buy them back one at a time. Two were already measured in segment A, and normality is the one left open, which the next slide closes. Bootstrap buys back normality; conformal avoids specifying a shape but substitutes exchangeability. Distribution-free never means assumption-free.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Not normal: the 80% band is too wide
text:
Not normal: the 80% band is too wide










Bars above the curve in the middle, still there out in the tails
The errors’ own middle 80% (blue) spans 36; \(c = 1.28\) claims 45


The check segment A put off: normality was item 4 and the only one unmarked.
Left panel is constant variance: a rolling SD that climbs while the pooled sigma-hat sits flat through the middle of it. One number standing in for a spread that tripled, too big for the 1980s and too small for the 2010s.
Right panel is a shape comparison, so make it one. The curve is a normal with the SAME SD as these residuals, so shape is the only thing that can differ. Trace where the bars leave it: well above in the middle, still there in the tails after the curve has gone flat. Too peaked and too fat-tailed at once, and no adjustment of the SD fixes that because the SD is already matched.
Then the two pairs of vertical lines, where the abstraction turns into money. Orange is where a normal of this SD puts the central 80%; blue is where these errors actually put it - narrower by about a fifth (36 against 45), which is exactly what segment D’s bootstrap comes back with.
Blue is also off-centre and someone will spot it: the +7.9 bias again. A symmetric plus-or-minus cannot represent that at all.
The fat tails cut the other way further out: at 95% the errors’ own span is about a tenth WIDER, 76 against 69. Sharp peak, fat tails, so the 80% band shrinks and the 95% does not - saying it here makes the bootstrap comparison a confirmation rather than a surprise. All three assumptions now fail; the next two methods each buy one back.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: The pool we draw from is the errors themselves
text:
The pool we draw from is the errors themselves










Write \(e^*\) for one picked out of these.
With replacement, so one of the 405 can be drawn twice


Read the two panels as one move, left to right. Left is the errors as they happened: one dot per month, at its distance from zero. Right is the same dots with the dates thrown away. Trace one orange line across the gap with your finger - it is flat, because the value survives and the date does not.
That flat line IS the assumption, so name it while it is on screen: a pool is what a series becomes once you decide the order does not matter. Everything in this segment is bought with that sentence.
Make it physical: 405 numbers in a hat, reach in, read one out, put it back. The vertical rule on each of the six is the size of that error, in dollars - the number the next slide adds to a forecast. Point out that they are still in the cloud on the right: that is what with replacement looks like, and it is the second bullet before you say it.
Then the right panel on its own. Same shape the normality check just failed on - sharp peak, long right tail. There it was evidence against a curve; here it is the thing we sample. Say the turn out loud: we stopped describing the shape and started using it. The recipe has not changed since segment C opened it; only the source of e has. Left to right in that panel means nothing; it is only spread so 405 dots do not sit on top of each other.
Someone will see the funnel on the left - the errors fan out as the series grows. Take it and park it: “good, hold that.” It is the closing slide of this segment, and it is the same growth the rolling SD showed two slides ago. Do not teach it here; the bootstrap has to win before it can be argued with.
Justify with replacement rather than asserting it, and the second reason is the real one. Arithmetic: 5,000 futures of 24 months is 120,000 draws out of 405 numbers, so there is no other option. Honest: we are treating those 405 as a sample of the errors this model makes, not a list of what will happen. Without replacement would be dealing out the past in a new order, a different claim entirely.
Have ready rather than teach: bootstrap_paths shifts the pool to mean zero first, so the +7.9 bias stays in the point forecast instead of sliding the band up with it.
If someone objects that reusing training errors is circular: we reuse their shape, not their order.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Forecast one step, add an error, feed it back
text:
Forecast one step, add an error, feed it back
A starred \(y^*\) is invented; a plain \(y\) was observed.

Each trip round the loop is \(y_t = \hat{y}_{t|t-1} + e_t\) again, one step further on:
\[\begin{aligned}
y^*_{T+1} &= \hat{y}_{T+1 \,|\, T}       + e^*_1 \\
y^*_{T+2} &= \hat{y}_{T+2 \,|\, T+1}     + e^*_2 \\
            &\;\;\vdots \\
y^*_{T+h} &= \hat{y}_{T+h \,|\, T+h-1}   + e^*_h
\end{aligned}\]



Every line after the first conditions on a \(y^*\) we invented
Run the loop out to \(h\) and that is one path


The model enters only through \(\hat{y}\): the loop bootstraps all five.


Draw the loop with your hand as you read the title: forecast, add, feed back, round again. Say the card early - nothing here is specific to the seasonal naive, which is what makes the loop worth learning.
The block is not a new claim: it is the recipe segment C opened with, run forward a step at a time. Every line has the same shape, and it is the shape they already agreed to.
Slow down on the conditioning bars, because that is where the whole segment turns. Line one forecasts from T, the end of the real data. Line two forecasts from T+1 - a value we made up one line ago. The model cannot tell a simulated value from a real one, so it just carries on, and from there the drawn errors compound: a value invented at step 1 is still inside every value after it.
Concrete if the room wants one: the seasonal naive copies last year’s same month, so its first twelve months still reach into real observations and month 13 is the first to copy an invented one. It then carries month 1’s error on top of its own, and month 25 carries three. That is segment C’s k+1 arriving by simulation instead of by derivation - two routes, one arithmetic - and it is why the next slide’s fan steps once a year.
Land the last bullet cleanly and stop: one trip round the loop is one step, the whole loop is ONE path, and one path is not an interval. That is the question the next slide answers.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Repeat 5000 times, then cut each column
text:
Repeat 5000 times, then cut each column










The band is not the method. The paths are. Pick one month, collect the 5,000 values the paths have there, sort them, and mark the 0.1 and the 0.9 quantile. Repeat at every month and the marks join up into the band. What a quantile is


Trace one path with your finger from the origin out to 24 months: one possible future, built by the recursion they just watched. Do it on a second and let them see a different future out of the same recipe.
The right panel is the same picture with more paths behind it, and the only new thing is the two orange lines. Stand at one month, look straight down the column of simulated values, sort them, cut where a tenth is left above and a tenth below. Do that at all 24 and you have the two lines.
Say the misconception the way the card does: students meet the bootstrap as a shaded band and assume the band is the method. The order of operations is the other way round.
Two things to point at. The cuts are jagged because the seasonal pattern is inside every path. And they are not equidistant from the middle - a quantile of a lopsided pile comes out lopsided, which plus-or-minus c sigma-hat cannot do at all.
The quantile link draws month 12’s column as its own histogram. Use it if the counting rule is where the room is stuck.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Dropping normality buys a fifth off the 80% band
text:
Dropping normality buys a fifth off the 80% band










Mean 80% width: 59.7 Gaussian vs 46.4 bootstrap, 22% narrower
Mean 95% width: 91.3 vs 90.1, the gap has closed


Same model, same point forecast, same data. Only the assumption changed, and the 80% band got a fifth narrower. That is the sharp peak paying off: the errors’ own middle 80% is tighter than the normal’s, so the empirical quantile beats the formula.
Notice the 95% bands barely differ, while the 80% bands do not. That is the shape of the residuals showing up exactly where you would expect it: the sharp peak makes the central 80% tighter, and the fat tails put the 95% back where the normal had it.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: The bootstrap trades normality for i.i.d.
text:
The bootstrap trades normality for i.i.d.










Normality is gone. Identically distributed is what bought it
One pool, two eras: the residual SD went 8.5 to 26.2
Draw from recent errors only and the 80% band widens, 46.4 to 81.2


Wider than the Gaussian’s 59.7 it just beat: the fifth was borrowed from the 1980s.


The previous slide was the win, so open by refusing to take it. Ask where the pool came from: every residual since 1982.
The same bootstrap twice, only the pool changed. Left draws from all 405 residuals, right from the last 120 - same model, same recursion, same point forecast. The right band is the honest one and it is 75% wider.
Say why, pointing back at the normality slide’s left panel: the spread tripled, 8.5 to 26.2. A pool mixing the 1980s with the 2010s draws 1980s-sized errors into a 2019 forecast. Identically distributed is the assumption doing the damage, and it is the one the bootstrap spent to buy normality back.
Then the card. Last slide’s headline was a fifth narrower than the Gaussian, 46.4 against 59.7. On an honest pool it is 81.2 - wider than the Gaussian it beat. The win was not a sharper method, it was a stale pool. The Gaussian at least states its constant-variance assumption out loud; the bootstrap hides the same one inside its pool.
Do not price the cost in coverage here - this slide is about width. Exercise 2.3 turns this exact knob, resid_tail, and reports what it does to coverage.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: The bootstrap’s one pool is the problem
text:
The bootstrap’s one pool is the problem
The bootstrap draws from one fixed pool of one-step residuals, shared by every horizon.


The errors change over time, so the pool mixes eras: 8.5 then, 26.2 now
The win it bought last segment was borrowed from the 1980s




Conformal’s answer: don’t assume one pool. Build a calibration set of \(h\)-step errors, one set per horizon, and assume only exchangeability.




One way to build the set: roll the origin and record the error at each horizon. The next slide is that, on a toy.


Open by refusing the bootstrap’s win, the way segment D’s last slide refused the Gaussian’s. The bootstrap draws from one fixed pool of one-step residuals, and that pool is the assumption doing the damage: it mixes the 1980s and the 2010s in one hat, so a 2019 forecast can draw a 1985-sized error. Last segment’s headline was a fifth narrower than the Gaussian; on an honest pool it was wider than the Gaussian it beat. The win was a stale pool, not a sharper method.
Conformal’s answer is the card: don’t assume one pool. Instead of one pool of one-step errors shared by every horizon, collect the h-step errors this model has already been caught making, one set per horizon, and assume only exchangeability. That is the whole idea; the rest of the segment is the mechanism.
The next slide is one way to build the set: roll the origin and record the error at each horizon. The toy there is the “how” this slide just promised.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: A 3-step error needs an origin and a horizon
text:
A 3-step error needs an origin and a horizon










Stand at \(t = 5\): pretend \(y_6 \dots y_{10}\) are gone, forecast three steps
Subtract what happened: \(e_{8|5} = y_8 - \hat{y}_{8|5}\)
A residual had one origin, yesterday. This error needs two indices
Slide the origin to \(t = 6, 7, \dots\) and collect: the calibration set


Walk this by hand on the numbers. Stand at t=5, the naive forecast for t=8 is whatever y_5 was, then look up what actually happened at t=8 and subtract. That single number is one member of the calibration set.
Slide the origin forward and you get another. That is the whole collection: stand, forecast, subtract, slide. The next slide writes down the quantile of those errors.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Take a quantile of the errors you collected
text:
Take a quantile of the errors you collected
\[\hat{y}_{T+h|T} \pm Q_{1-\alpha}\big(|e_{t+h|t}|\big)\]

\(Q_{1-\alpha}\) is the \((1-\alpha)\) quantile of the errors just collected, so 80% takes \(\alpha = 0.2\)
One quantile per \(h\), so band growth is measured, not assumed: segment C’s width formulas are not needed
No \(\hat{\sigma}\) and no normal table, so this works on a model with no interval formula at all



The price is exchangeability: shuffle the calibration errors and nothing changes. Weaker than the bootstrap’s i.i.d., but a variance that keeps climbing still breaks it.


Exchangeability asks whether the calibration errors and the next error remain comparable when their order is shuffled. It permits dependence that i.i.d. forbids, but does not excuse a changing regime (e.g. non-constant variance over decades).
The interval is an empirical quantile of collected absolute errors: no sigma-hat to estimate, no normal table to look up. Because the width comes out of the data at each h separately, the staircase, the square-root-h, the drift formula: none of segment C’s width machinery is needed. That is also why conformal intervals work on models that have no closed-form formula (ML models, neural nets, Day 3).
The next slide collects those errors into a grid, one column per horizon, and cuts each column.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Collect them into a grid, then cut each column
text:
Collect them into a grid, then cut each column










Segment D cut columns of futures it invented. This cuts columns of errors the model actually made. What a quantile is


Say the card first, because it is the only new idea on the slide. The move is the one they watched five minutes ago on the bootstrap band: stand at one horizon, look down the column, sort, cut. Nothing about that has changed. What changed is what is in the column.
Left panel, and take it slowly. One row per forecast origin, one column per horizon, 8 by 24, and every cell is one error the seasonal naive made from that origin at that distance. Walk the top row across with your hand: stand in 2000, forecast 24 months, record how wrong each one was.
The 2008 row is dark the whole way across and someone will ask. Turnover went from 219 in Dec 2008 to 340 in Dec 2009 and never came back, so every forecast made from that origin is wrong by a lot. Do not treat it as a blemish - it is the reason the right-hand panel looks the way it does, and exercise 2.3c has them meet the same +120.8 by hand.
Right panel is the cut. Eight numbers, reflected to both signs so there are 16, sorted low to high. The 90% cut lands BETWEEN rank 14 and rank 15 - point at the gap. That is what a quantile of sixteen numbers has to do, and it is the whole explanation of the jitter the next two slides show.
The open circles are worth ten seconds: the reflection is not extra data, it is the same eight numbers with a minus sign. Which means the band is symmetric whatever the errors do - the bootstrap could lean and this cannot. Bank it; the assumptions table at the end of the deck collects it.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Conformal found the staircase without the formula
text:
Conformal found the staircase without the formula










Year 1: 48.4 wide, against the formula’s 49.5
Year 2: 70.0 against 70.0, the same number
Nobody told it \(m = 12\). It found the step by counting
Horizon to horizon it wanders, because each column holds 16 numbers


This is the segment’s payoff, so do not let it go by as another chart. Segment C spent a whole slide deriving root k+1 from the seasonal naive’s recursion. This line was never shown that derivation, never told the period is twelve, never told there is a staircase. Ask the room where it steps before you say anything.
Then the two pairs of dashed means. Year one 48.4 against 49.5, year two 70.0 against 70.0. Ratio 1.45 measured, 1.41 derived. Two completely different routes to the same number, which is the strongest evidence in the deck that segment C’s derivation was not bookkeeping.
Do not oversell it. The orange line is jagged and one horizon can be a third off its neighbour - it agrees on the average and disagrees everywhere. Say why in the same breath as the third bullet: 16 numbers per column, and a quantile of sixteen numbers moves when any one of them moves. The next slide is that sentence with a knob on it.
If someone asks which is better here: neither, and that is the point. They agree because the assumption happens to hold well enough on this series. On a series where it does not, only one of them notices.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: More origins buy a steadier band from a staler regime
text:
More origins buy a steadier band from a staler regime










Mean 80% width 74.3 at 4 windows, 59.2 at 8, 50.0 at 16
16 windows reaches back to 1984: residual SD 8.5 then, 26.2 now


Segment D’s pool argument in different clothes: more calibration data is a steadier quantile drawn from a staler regime.


Open by refusing the last slide’s win, the way you refused the bootstrap’s. Where did the eight origins come from, and why eight?
Three lines, same method, same model, same point forecast - only the calibration set changed. Blue is four origins and it is violent: 74.3 on average and one horizon nearly double its neighbour. Grey is sixteen and it is smooth and narrow, 50.0. If narrow and smooth were the goal, sixteen wins and the slide is over.
So make them look at the legend, which is where the cost is. Sixteen windows reaches back to 1984. That is the 1980s pool again - the era whose residual SD was 8.5 against today’s 26.2 - and this time it arrives through the calibration set rather than through the bootstrap’s hat. Same mistake, different door.
That is the card, and it is the honest reading of exchangeability. Shuffling the calibration errors has to change nothing. Errors from 1985 and errors from 2018 are not exchangeable on this series, and no amount of distribution-free machinery fixes that, because it was never a distributional assumption.
One implementation note to drop in before the lab: n_windows is a request, not a count. Under 193 points statsforecast silently calibrates on fewer windows than you asked for, and says nothing.
Eight is the course’s choice and it is a judgement, not a default: far enough back for the quantile to mean something, not so far back that it is measuring a different series. Say that out loud - students will otherwise read 8 as a setting that came with the library.
The next slide is the one line that gives any model an interval.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Any model at all can be given a conformal interval
text:
Any model at all can be given a conformal interval
from statsforecast.utils import ConformalIntervals

# the grid from two slides back: n_windows is its rows, h its columns
ci = ConformalIntervals(n_windows=8, h=24)

sf_conf = StatsForecast(
    models=[SeasonalNaive(season_length=12, prediction_intervals=ci)],
    freq="MS",
)
fc_conf = sf_conf.forecast(df=train, h=24, level=[80, 95])

Nothing here names a distribution, so it works on a model with no interval formula


The practical close of the segment, and what a Day 3 author needs: any model without a closed-form interval gets one from prediction_intervals=ConformalIntervals(…). That is the line Day 3 reaches for every time a model has no formula, which by then is most of them.
Point at the ConformalIntervals call and back at the grid. Those two arguments ARE the grid: n_windows is its rows, h is its columns. Nothing else in the call has anything to do with intervals.
The reflection bullet is the one to slow down on, because it is a real limitation stated as a fact about the code. The seasonal naive’s residuals are biased +7.9 and skewed, the bootstrap band leaned to match, and this one cannot - plus-or-minus one quantile is symmetric whatever went in. Distribution-free bought the shape of the tails and gave back the lean.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Three methods, three bands, one centre line
text:
Three methods, three bands, one centre line










Mean 80% width: Gaussian 59.7, bootstrap 46.4, conformal 59.2


One point forecast, three bands. Left panel says they are not the same object; right panel says how they differ in width and smoothness. All three find the seasonal step: the bootstrap is the Gaussian’s staircase shifted down, narrower but the same shape, because it simulates the same recursion. The conformal is the same step on average but jittery, because each column holds only 16 numbers. Same centre line throughout.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Every interval method spends an assumption
text:
Every interval method spends an assumption








Method
Assumes
Gives




Gaussian
uncorrelated · constant variance · normal
closed form


Bootstrap
uncorrelated · one fixed error pool
any error shape


Conformal
exchangeable \(h\)-step errors
no shape, but a symmetric band









Important


Pick by which assumption you can defend, not by the widths on the last slide.




The table is the takeaway. Each row is a trade, and the honest question when choosing is not “which is most accurate” but “which of these three assumptions am I willing to make about this series”.
If the room wants a default: conformal, because it assumes least, and because it is the one that generalises to models that have no formula. That is also why it is the one Day 3 will lean on. But say both qualifications out loud. Its interval is distribution-free, not assumption-free, and the n_windows slide showed a changing error regime breaking exchangeability on this very series. And the third column is a trade too, not a ranking: only the bootstrap can give back a band that leans, which on a model biased +7.9 is not nothing.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Reminder: a quantile is a counting rule
text:
Reminder: a quantile is a counting rule
Sort the values. A quantile is then just a position in that list: \(0.5n\) is the median, \(0.9n\) is the \(0.9\) quantile, \(0.1n\) is the \(0.1\) quantile.










One sort, three positions. The 80% interval is the span between the \(0.1n\) and \(0.9n\) cuts, taken again at every month. Back


Off the flow, after the closing slide, reached by a link from segment C’s opening slide or the bootstrap band. Back returns to whichever you came from; Alt+Left does the same. Use it if the room needs it, skip it otherwise.
Start from the median and generalise by changing one number. Sort the list, take the middle: position 0.5 times n. Ask for the 0.9 quantile and nothing changes but the 0.5, which becomes 0.9. Same for 0.1. One rule with a knob on it.
Say “half the list”, not “half the range” - the median is the middle by count, and on these skewed paths the midpoint of the range is nowhere near it.
Read it off the picture: the grey line is the median at position 2,500 of 5,000, the dashed lines are 500 and 4,500. The same three cuts land on the histogram on the right, and the shaded span is the middle 80% the fan chart draws.
Leave them with this: a quantile is a position in a sorted list, not a formula.

title: Benchmarks, Residuals & Prediction Intervals
section: Reminder: a standard deviation is a width
text:
Reminder: a standard deviation is a width
The standard deviation is one number: how far a typical value sits from the middle.










The Gaussian band is this width times \(c\): 1.28 for an 80% interval. Back


Off the flow, after the closing slide, reached from the sigma-hat slide’s link; Back returns to it.
These are the actual residuals segment A has been reading, not a toy. The SD is one number for how far a typical residual sits from the middle, in millions of turnover, and the shaded bands are one and two of them either side.
Read the shares off the labels rather than reciting 68 and 95 - on these residuals they are close but not equal, and that gap is what the normality slide is about.
Connect it to the formula behind: the Gaussian interval is this width times 1.28 for an 80% band. Everything else in segment C argues about whether that is the right width.

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: Day 2 ended with a floor. Today we go after it
text:
Day 2 ended with a floor. Today we go after it

Parts A to C: one model, built in three steps, on states you already know
Part D: the family those three steps belong to, and how it picks a member
Part E: the same harness Day 2 built, pointed at a model it has never seen








The floor to beat


Seasonal naive, MASE 1.18, scaled CRPS 0.031, over eight rolling folds. Its residuals fail Ljung-Box at \(p \approx 10^{-240}\), so it is beatable.




Open by putting yesterday’s last slide back up in words. They left with a scoring harness they wrote themselves and a seasonal naive on top of everything it measured, at MASE 1.18 and scaled CRPS 0.031. And they left with the reason to keep going: those residuals are nowhere near white noise, so there is structure in this series that none of the five benchmarks captured.
Today is one model, taught properly, and then one framework that runs a dozen of them for you. The order matters: by the time the framework appears this afternoon, every model inside it is one they have either built or watched get built.
Set the expectation about the result honestly, because it is coming in Part E and it is not a landslide. ETS will beat the floor on the point forecast by about half a percent and lose to it on the distribution. That is a normal result in this field, and diagnosing it is the whole exercise.

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: Your benchmarks are two ends of one dial
text:
Your benchmarks are two ends of one dial

Naiveall the weight on \(y_T\) somewhere in betweenrecent counts more, old still counts Meanequal weight on every \(y_t\)


The naive forecast says the last observation is all that matters. The mean says a point from start of the series matters exactly as much as last point.

This is the slide that makes exponential smoothing feel inevitable rather than invented. Both of yesterday’s simplest benchmarks are weighted averages of the history. They just sit at opposite extremes of the same dial.
Ask the room which one is closer to right for the takeaway food series. Most will say the naive, and they are right, which is exactly why the seasonal naive was yesterday’s best benchmark. But nobody actually believes that only December 2018 carries information about December 2019.
The obvious repair is a weighted average where recent observations count more and the weight fades as you go back. That is the whole idea, and it has a name.

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: Simple exponential smoothing is the dial between them
text:
Simple exponential smoothing is the dial between them
\[\hat{y}_{T+1|T} = \alpha y_T + \alpha(1-\alpha) y_{T-1} + \alpha(1-\alpha)^2 y_{T-2} + \cdots\]
The weights shrink geometrically as you go back.



\(\alpha\) near 1
Fast to react. Almost the naive forecast.

\(\alpha\) near 0
Slow and smooth. Approaches the mean.


One parameter, alpha, between 0 and 1. It is the smoothing parameter, and it sets how fast the weight decays as you walk backwards through the history.
Point at the two columns and connect them to the previous slide: alpha equal to 1 puts a weight of exactly 1 on the last observation and zero on everything else, which is the naive forecast. Push alpha towards 0 and the weights flatten out towards the mean.
The word “exponential” in the name is the geometric decay, nothing more exotic. If anyone asks why the weights sum to 1, that is the geometric series alpha times the sum of (1 minus alpha) to the j, which is exactly 1.

\(\alpha\) is fitted
Pick the \(\alpha\) and the starting level \(\ell_0\) that minimize the sum of squared one-step errors on the training data:
\[\text{SSE} = \sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(y_t - \hat{y}_{t|t-1}\right)^2\]

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: SES on its own gives you a flat line
text:
SES on its own gives you a flat line










One state, and it is a level. There is nothing in this model that knows the series is growing.

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: Holt keeps two numbers
text:
Holt keeps two numbers
Think of Holt as maintaining two pieces of information:
\[\boxed{\text{What is the series worth right now?}} \;\longrightarrow\; \ell_t\]
\[\boxed{\text{How fast is it changing?}} \;\longrightarrow\; b_t\]

\[\text{future value} \;\approx\; \text{current value} + (\text{rate of change}) \times (\text{time ahead})\]

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: A second state gives the forecast a slope
text:
A second state gives the forecast a slope
\[\ell_t = \alpha y_t + (1-\alpha)\;\boxed{\,\ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1}\,} \qquad\text{(level)}\] \[b_t = \beta^*(\ell_t - \ell_{t-1}) + (1-\beta^*) b_{t-1} \qquad\text{(slope)}\] \[\hat{y}_{t+h|t} = \ell_t + h b_t \qquad\text{(forecast)}\]

Put \(h = 1\) in the last line, one step earlier: the boxed term is the forecast Holt already made for \(y_t\).
\[\hat{y}_{t|t-1} = \ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\ell_t = \alpha\,y_t + (1-\alpha)\,\hat{y}_{t|t-1}\]

That is the SES level equation unchanged: step from what you predicted towards what you saw. Only the prediction learned a slope.


The slide already shows the h = 1 derivation; the only new thing is the box. The level update now starts from where the trend said it would be, not where it was, and that box is the only difference from SES.
That is word for word the SES level equation, because in SES the one-step forecast was just the level. Nothing about the update changed when the trend arrived; the prediction inside it got better. Say that out loud, because Part C adds seasonality and the level equation will survive that too.
Beta-star is a second smoothing parameter with the same meaning as alpha: how fast does the model revise its belief about the slope when the data disagrees. It is fitted alongside alpha and the two initial states.
The pattern is the thing to notice. Every state in this family is updated by the same move: a weighted step from what you believed towards what you just saw.

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: Holt adds a slope but not a December
text:
Holt adds a slope but not a December










Better, and still wrong in an obvious way.


The line now rises, which is progress you can see. Over 24 months it climbs from about 356 to about 373, which is roughly the right slope for this series.
And it is still a straight line through a series that visibly swings by 30 percent between February and December. The residuals from this model would fail every diagnostic in yesterday’s lecture, for a reason the picture already gives away.
Two states means two things remembered. Nothing here knows where it is in the cycle.

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: Extrapolate a straight line far enough and it lies
text:
Extrapolate a straight line far enough and it lies









At \(h = 60\) the two disagree by about 38 units, on a series whose last observation was 393.

Empirically, forecasts that extrapolate a constant slope forever are too optimistic at long horizons. Hyndman’s damped trend is the standard repair and it is one extra parameter.
The damping parameter phi sits between 0 and 1 and multiplies the slope at every step out, so the contributions form a geometric series that converges. The forecast approaches a horizontal asymptote instead of running off the top of the chart.
Point at the gap at the right edge. Five years out, the undamped line has added 38 units that the damped one has not. Neither is verified here, and that is the point: nothing in the training data can tell you which is right five years out, so the conservative one is the better default.

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: Damping turns the slope sum into a geometric series
text:
Damping turns the slope sum into a geometric series
\[\hat{y}_{t+h|t} = \ell_t + h\,b_t \qquad\text{(undamped)}\] \[\hat{y}_{t+h|t} = \ell_t + (\phi + \phi^2 + \cdots + \phi^h)\,b_t \qquad\text{(damped)}\]

With \(\phi < 1\) that sum converges, so the forecast has a ceiling:
\[\hat{y}_{t+h|t} \;\longrightarrow\; \ell_t + \frac{\phi}{1-\phi}\,b_t\]

Same move as the SES slide, pointed the other way. There they unrolled the recursion backwards over the history and the weights fell out. Here you unroll the forecast forwards over the horizon, and what falls out is the flattening they just watched.
The slide does the unrolling; the point is that a geometric series with ratio below 1 has a finite sum, so the forecast has a ceiling.
Write the ceiling on the board if it helps: phi over one minus phi. It is worth computing one value live, because the numbers surprise people. At 0.9 the model can only ever add nine slopes to the current level, no matter how far out you ask. That is a hard cap on the forecast, chosen by one parameter.
Then set up the next slide’s bullet about 0.8. Phi of 0.8 caps the whole forecast at four slopes, which on monthly data is gone inside half a year. That is why fitted phi almost always lands high, between 0.8 and 0.98, and why anything much lower means the trend has effectively been switched off.

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: The third state updates like the other two
text:
The third state updates like the other two
The forecast gains one term: the matching value from the last cycle.
\[\hat{y}_{t+h|t} = \ell_t + h\,b_t + \underbrace{s_{t+h-m(k+1)}}_{\text{the matching season value}}\]

From Day 2 take the trend out, keep what is left:
\[y_t - \underbrace{(\ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1})}_{\text{trend}} \;=\; \text{the season this period}\]


\[s_t = \gamma\,(y_t - \ell_{t-1} - b_{t-1}) + (1-\gamma)\,s_{t-m} \qquad\text{(season)}\]

Read it in the order it is built. The forecast needs a season value, so the state has to hold one per position in the cycle: twelve of them for monthly data, each refreshed once per cycle rather than once per step.
The middle line is Day 2’s decomposition, written as one line. There they subtracted a fitted trend and called the remainder seasonal; here the level and slope are the trend, and the remainder is the raw season value for this period.
The last line is the same weighted step they have now seen three times, and the level and slope equations do not change at all. They work on the observation with its season removed, y minus s at t minus m, exactly as in Part B.
The k in the forecast subscript just counts complete cycles; do not spend more than a sentence on it.
Gamma is worth one question out loud: how much should one unusual year change what the model believes about that point in the cycle?

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: Additive or multiplicative is a real choice
text:
Additive or multiplicative is a real choice


Additive season
\(y_t = \ell_t + s_t\)
A season adds the same number of units, whatever the level is.

Multiplicative season
\(y_t = \ell_t \times s_t\)
A season is a fixed percentage of the level.








What the spine does


Its seasonal swing grew from a few units in the 1980s to about 55 by 2018, right alongside the level.




This is the choice Day 1 already made them look at, in different clothes. When they log-transformed this series in lecture 2, the reason was that the seasonal swings grow with the level. Same observation, now a model decision.
The numbers in the callout are read off the fitted seasonal state, which is on screen a few slides from now, so this is a promise the deck keeps.
There are two ways out and the course teaches both: model the season as multiplicative, or transform the data until the season is additive. Part D does that pair properly.

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: Holt-Winters has the right shape
text:
Holt-Winters has the right shape










Flat, then tilted, then the right shape. One state added per slide.


Compare the Holt-Winters line against the dashed holdout. It puts the peaks and the troughs in the right places and at roughly the right size. It is not perfect and it does not need to be.
If someone asks whether this beats the seasonal naive: good question, hold it for Part E, because answering it properly needs eight folds and not this chart.

ETS(A,N,N) is SES. ETS(A,A,N) is Holt. ETS(A,A,A) is additive Holt-Winters. Parts A, B and C, renamed.



Two errors, five trends, three seasons: about thirty models, and you have already built three of them.


Do not teach this table row by row. Put it up, say what the three letters are, and spend the time on the line underneath, which is the payoff.
The one thing worth saying about the error letter, because it is the least intuitive: an additive error is a fixed number of units, a multiplicative error is a fixed percentage. On a series that grew by a factor of eight, that distinction is not cosmetic.
A handful of the thirty are unstable and get excluded, which is why the card says “about”.

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: The error term makes it a model
text:
The error term makes it a model
Holt-Winters gives one number. ETS also says where the randomness enters.
\[y_t = \underbrace{\ell_{t-1} + b_{t-1} + s_{t-m}}_{\text{what the states predict}} \;+\; \underbrace{\varepsilon_t}_{\text{the error}}\]

Now the model can say how likely the data it saw was. That number is its likelihood, and it is what lets you rank models.



It can also draw many futures instead of one line. The spread of those futures is the interval.


This is the answer to “why not just use Holt-Winters and stop”. The point forecasts are identical. What the state space form adds is the error term.
Connect it to yesterday explicitly. To get an interval out of a seasonal naive they had to supply an assumption: Gaussian errors, bootstrapped residuals, or conformal calibration. ETS carries its own error distribution instead, so the interval is part of the model, and it emits quantiles directly.
That is exactly why Part E can score it on scaled CRPS without a line of new plumbing.

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: AICc picks one member of the family
text:
AICc picks one member of the family
\[\text{AICc} = \underbrace{-2\log L}_{\text{how badly it fits}} \;+\; \underbrace{2k}_{\text{a toll per parameter}} \;+\; \text{a small-sample correction}\]

A bigger model always fits better, so fit alone would always pick the biggest one. The toll makes it pay for every parameter it asks for.



Lower is better, only the gaps between models mean anything, and AutoETS keeps the smallest.


Read the formula left to right in two beats. Minus two log-likelihood is the misfit and it falls as the model explains more. Two k is the toll: every parameter costs two points, whether or not it earned them.
The correction is what the extra c stands for, it matters at small sample sizes, and at 441 observations it is a rounding error. Do not spend time on it.
The caveat worth stating: the number only compares models fit to the same data. It says nothing about whether any of them is good, only which is best, which is why Part E still scores the winner out of sample.

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: The season changes the score. The trend does not
text:
The season changes the score. The trend does not










Drop the season and the score jumps by hundreds. Add a trend and it hardly moves.


Every bar here is a real fit on the spine, and the axis is the distance from the winner rather than the raw AICc, because the raw numbers are all near 4500 and only the differences matter.
Read the shape, not the values. The two models with no seasonal letter sit about 475 points out. Among the four seasonal ones, adding a trend moves the score by 16 points one way and 7 the other.
Same conclusion Day 1 reached from the ACF: on retail data, seasonality is what discriminates.

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: What it picked has no trend term
text:
What it picked has no trend term


selected      : ETS(M,N,A)
alpha (level) : 0.525
gamma (season): 0.321



Multiplicative error, no trend state, additive season. On a series that grew by a factor of eight.


This is the slide that earns the segment, so give it room and let the room react before explaining it.
The explanation is in the level equation from Part A. With alpha at 0.52, the level takes a half-step towards every new observation, so it climbs perfectly well on its own. A trend state would let the model extrapolate that climb, and that is the part AICc rejected: two more parameters, and a slope that has to be right twelve months out.
Connect it to Part B’s callout. This is what “damping loses on this series” looked like from the other end: the search did not merely damp the trend, it removed it.
The lesson worth naming: an automatic search optimizes the criterion you gave it, not the story you had in your head.

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: The states it learned are a decomposition
text:
The states it learned are a decomposition










The level climbed without a trend state, and the season grew from a few units in the 1980s to about 55 by 2018.


Deliberately the same picture Day 1 drew with STL, in the same panel vocabulary, because these are the same kind of object.
The season panel pays the promise made three slides back: a few units in the 1980s, plus 55 by 2018. That is multiplicative behaviour showing up inside an additive seasonal state, and the model copes with it through the multiplicative error term, which is the next slide’s subject.
If anyone asks why the season panel is noisier late in the series: the swings are bigger in absolute terms, so a fixed percentage of noise is a bigger number.

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: Two ways to handle a season that grows
text:
Two ways to handle a season that grows


Change the data
Transform until the swings hold still, forecast, then transform back. Day 1 used the log.

Change the model
A multiplicative error already works in percentages. This is what AutoETS chose here.


\[w_t = \begin{cases} \log(y_t) & \lambda = 0 \\ (y_t^{\lambda}-1)/\lambda & \lambda \neq 0\end{cases}\]
Box-Cox is one dial across the transforms: \(\lambda = 1\) is none, \(\lambda = 0\) is the log.

The two columns are the honest summary of the choice. Both routes handle variance that grows with the level. Transforming is more explicit and leaves you owning the back-transformation. Letting the error be multiplicative is one letter in the model name.
Do not present either as correct. They are the same idea entering the model at two different points, and this course took the second route by accident, because it let the search choose.

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: ETS wins on one window and ties over eight folds
text:
ETS wins on one window and ties over eight folds










One window: 0.97 against 1.11. Eight folds: 1.176 against 1.183, inside a fold spread of 0.72 to 2.02.


This is Exercise 2.4 and 2.5 happening again, to a different model, and it is worth saying so out loud before explaining the chart.
Left panel: on the single 24-month window ETS improves on the seasonal naive by 13 percent, the kind of number that gets a model shipped. Over eight folds both land on 1.18 and the win evaporates. Yesterday the decomposition route did exactly this, in exactly this direction, on this same series.
Right panel is why. The fold-to-fold spread runs from about 0.72 to about 2.02 for both models, so a 0.007 difference in the means is a small fraction of the difference between a good year and a bad one.
If someone asks whether the win is real: eight folds cannot settle a gap this size, and the next move is more folds or more series, not a louder claim. That is why score_cv returns mase_min and mase_max.

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: Its 80% band covers 87.5%
text:
Its 80% band covers 87.5%










More coverage than promised is not better. It means the band is too wide.


Both bars miss, in opposite directions, and the ETS miss is the interesting one because it looks like good news. The chart calls a band honest within five points of nominal, which the seasonal naive clears and ETS does not.
Ask the room which model they would rather ship, before explaining. Most rooms pick the 87.5 percent, because more coverage sounds safer.
A band that claims 80 and delivers 87.5 is wrong by 7.5 points, and it is wrong in the direction that costs money: every decision sized off it is hedged more than the evidence requires.
Recall yesterday’s rule while it is on screen: coverage checks a band, it cannot rank two bands. To rank them you need a proper score.

title: Exponential Smoothing & ETS
section: The wider band scores worse
text:
The wider band scores worse










ETS has the wider band on the left and the worse CRPS on the right.


This is exactly yesterday’s STL comparison run in reverse, and it is worth saying so. Yesterday the decomposition route had the narrowest bands and the worst coverage and still lost on CRPS. Today ETS has the widest bands and the most coverage and still loses on CRPS.
Neither sharpness nor coverage ranks a forecast on its own. CRPS does, because it scores the whole distribution against what actually happened.
The seasonal naive is not on top here because it is clever. It is on top because its band is roughly the right size and roughly in the right place.
